Claude Code isn't just a tool for writing code - it's designed to work alongside you throughout every phase of a software project. Think of it as another engineer on your team who can handle everything from initial setup to deployment and support.
The /init Command

When you start working with Claude Code on a project, the first thing you'll want to do is run the /init command. This tells Claude to scan your entire codebase and understand your project's structure, dependencies, coding style, and architecture.

Claude summarizes everything it learns in a special file called CLAUDE.md. This file automatically gets included as context in all future conversations, so Claude remembers important details about your project.
You can have multiple CLAUDE.md files for different scopes:
Project - Shared between all engineers working on the project
Local - Your personal notes that aren't checked into git
User - Used across all your projects

When running /init, you can add special directions for areas you want Claude to focus on. The generated file will include build commands, coding guidelines, and project-specific patterns that Claude should follow.
To add a note later, ask Claude to put it in your CLAUDE.md file. For example: Add "Always use descriptive variable names" to CLAUDE.md. You can also run /memory to open the file yourself.
Common Workflows
Claude works best when you approach it as an effort multiplier. The more context and structure you provide, the better results you'll get. Here's the most effective workflow:
Step 1: Feed Context into Claude

Before asking Claude to build something, identify files in your codebase that are relevant to the feature you want to create. Ask Claude to read and analyze these files first. This gives Claude examples of your coding patterns and existing functionality it can build upon.
Step 2: Tell Claude to Plan a Solution

Instead of jumping straight to implementation, ask Claude to think through the problem and create a plan. Tell Claude specifically not to write any code yet - just focus on the approach and steps needed.
Step 3: Ask Claude to Implement the Solution
Once you have a solid plan, ask Claude to implement it. Claude will write code based on the context and planning work you've already done together.
Test-Driven Development Workflow
For even better results, you can use a test-driven approach:
Feed context into Claude - Same as before, show Claude relevant files
Ask Claude to think of test cases - Have Claude brainstorm what tests would validate your new feature
Ask Claude to implement those tests - Select the most relevant tests and have Claude write them
Ask Claude to write code that passes the tests - Claude will iterate on the implementation until all tests pass
This approach often produces more robust code because Claude has clear success criteria to work toward.
Practical Example
Here's how these workflows look in practice. Let's say you want to add a document conversion tool to an existing project:
CODE:

// First, ask Claude to read relevant files > Read the math.py and document.py files // Then ask for planning (not implementation) > Plan to implement document_path_to_markdown tool: 1. Create a function that: - Takes a file path parameter - Validates the file exists - Determines file type from extension - Reads binary data from file - Leverages existing binary_document_to_markdown function - Returns markdown string 2. Add appropriate documentation 3. Register the tool with MCP server 4. Add tests // Finally, ask for implementation > Implement the plan
Claude will then create the function, update the necessary files, write tests, and even run the test suite to verify everything works correctly.
Additional Commands
Claude Code includes several helpful commands:
/clear - Clears conversation history and resets context
/init - Scans codebase and creates CLAUDE.md documentation
/memory - Opens your CLAUDE.md files for editing

Claude can also handle routine development tasks like staging and committing changes to git, running tests, and managing dependencies. Instead of switching between your editor and terminal, you can ask Claude to handle these tasks while you focus on the bigger picture.

The key to success with Claude Code is remembering that it's designed to be a collaborative partner, not just a code generator. The more context and structure you provide, the more effectively Claude can help you build and maintain your projects.
Loading

Claude Code has an MCP client built right into it, which means you can connect MCP servers to dramatically expand what Claude can do. This opens up some really powerful possibilities for customizing your development workflow.
How MCP Extends Claude

The Model Context Protocol allows Claude Code to connect to external services and tools through MCP servers. Instead of being limited to Claude's built-in capabilities, you can add custom functionality by connecting servers that provide specific tools, resources, or integrations.
Each MCP server can expose different types of functionality to Claude through three main components: Tools (for taking actions), Prompts (for templates), and Resources (for accessing data).
Setting Up an MCP Server
Adding an MCP server to Claude Code is straightforward. You use the command line to register your server:
bash
CODE:
claude mcp add [server-name] [command-to-start-server]
For example, if you have a document processing server that starts with uv run main.py, you'd run:
bash
CODE:
claude mcp add documents uv run main.py
Once registered, Claude Code will automatically connect to your server when it starts up.
Example: Document Processing

A practical example is creating a tool that lets Claude read PDF and Word documents. By building an MCP server with a "document_path_to_markdown" tool, you can ask Claude to convert document contents to markdown format.
When you ask Claude to "Convert the tests/fixtures/mcp_docs.docx file to markdown", it will automatically use your custom tool to read the document and return the converted content.
Popular MCP Integrations
The MCP ecosystem includes servers for many common development tools and services:
sentry-mcp - Automatically discover and fix bugs logged in Sentry
playwright-mcp - Gives Claude browser automation capabilities for testing and troubleshooting
figma-context-mcp - Exposes Figma designs to Claude
mcp-atlassian - Allows Claude to access Confluence and Jira
firecrawl-mcp-server - Adds web scraping capabilities to Claude
slack-mcp - Allows Claude to post messages or reply to specific threads
Building Your Development Workflow
The real power comes from combining multiple MCP servers that match your specific development process. You might set up:
A Sentry server to fetch production error details
A Jira server to read ticket requirements
A Slack server to notify your team when work is complete
Custom servers for your internal tools and APIs

This creates a development environment where Claude can seamlessly work with all the tools and services you already use, making it a much more powerful coding assistant tailored to your specific workflow.
Loading

Workflows and agents are strategies for handling user tasks that can't be completed by Claude in a single request. You've actually been creating both throughout this course - when you used tools and let Claude figure out how to complete tasks, that was an agent.
When to Use Workflows vs Agents
The decision comes down to how well you understand the task:
Use workflows when you can picture the exact flow or steps that Claude should go through to solve a problem, or when your app's UX constrains users to a set of tasks
Use agents when you're not sure exactly what task or task parameters you'll give to Claude

Workflows are a series of calls to Claude meant to solve a specific problem through a predetermined series of steps. Agents give Claude a goal and a set of tools, expecting Claude to figure out how to complete the goal through the provided tools.
Example: Image to CAD Workflow
Let's look at a practical workflow example. Imagine building a web app where users drag and drop an image of a metal part, and you create a STEP file (an industry standard for 3D models) from it.

Since we have a pretty good idea of exactly what to do when a user supplies an image file, and we can easily write all of this out with code as a predefined series of steps, this makes a perfect workflow candidate.
Here's how the workflow breaks down:
Feed an image into Claude, asking it to describe the object
Based on the description, ask Claude to use the CadQuery library to model the object
Create a rendering
Ask Claude to grade the rendering against the original image. If there are issues, fix them
The Evaluator-Optimizer Pattern
This modeling workflow is an example of an evaluator-optimizer pattern. Here's how it works:
Producer: Takes input and creates output (Claude using CadQuery to model the part and create a rendering)
Grader: Evaluates the output against some criteria
Feedback loop: If the grader doesn't accept the output, feedback goes back to the producer for improvement
Iteration: The cycle repeats until the grader accepts the output
Why Learn Workflow Patterns

The goal of identifying different workflows is to give you a set of repeatable recipes for implementing your own features. The Evaluator-Optimizer is one workflow pattern that has worked well for other engineers - consider using it in your own app!

Remember, identifying workflows doesn't inherently do anything for us - we still have to write the actual code to implement them. But these patterns have proven successful for many engineers, so they're worth understanding and applying to your own projects.
Loading

When building AI applications, you'll often encounter tasks that seem simple on the surface but become complex when you try to implement them effectively. Let's explore a powerful pattern called parallelization workflows that can help you break down complex tasks into manageable, focused pieces.
The Problem with Complex Single Prompts

Imagine you're building a material designer application where users upload images of parts and receive recommendations for the best material to use. Your first instinct might be to send the image to Claude with a simple prompt asking it to choose between metal, polymer, ceramic, composite, elastomer, or wood.

While this approach might work, you're asking Claude to do a lot of heavy lifting in a single request. Without specific criteria for each material type, the results won't be as reliable as they could be.

You might think to improve this by adding detailed criteria for each material into one massive prompt. But this creates a new problem - Claude has to juggle all these different considerations simultaneously, which can lead to confusion and suboptimal results.
A Better Approach: Parallelization

Instead of cramming everything into one request, you can split the task into multiple parallel requests. Each request focuses on evaluating the part for a single material type with specialized criteria.
Here's how it works:
Send the same image to Claude multiple times simultaneously
Each request includes specialized criteria for one material (metal criteria, polymer criteria, ceramic criteria, etc.)
Claude evaluates the part's suitability for each material independently
Collect all the analysis results and feed them into a final aggregation step
The final step sends all the individual analysis results back to Claude with a request to compare them and make a final material recommendation.
How Parallelization Workflows Work
The parallelization pattern follows a simple structure:
Split a single task into multiple sub-tasks - Break down the complex decision into focused, specialized evaluations
Run the sub-tasks in parallel - Execute all evaluations simultaneously for faster processing
Aggregate the results together - Combine the specialized analyses into a final decision
The parallelized sub-tasks don't need to be identical - Each can have a specialized prompt, set of tools, or evaluation criteria
Benefits of This Approach
Parallelization workflows offer several key advantages:

Focused attention: Claude can concentrate on one specific aspect at a time rather than trying to balance multiple competing considerations simultaneously. This leads to more thorough and accurate analysis for each material type.

Easier optimization: You can improve and test the prompts for each material evaluation independently. If your metal analysis isn't working well, you can refine just that prompt without affecting the others.

Better scalability: Adding new materials to evaluate is straightforward - just add another parallel request. You don't need to rewrite existing prompts or worry about how the new criteria might interfere with existing ones.
Improved reliability: By breaking down the complex task, you reduce the cognitive load on the AI model and get more consistent, reliable results.
When to Use Parallelization

This pattern works well when you have a complex decision that can be broken down into independent evaluations. Look for situations where you're asking an AI to consider multiple criteria, compare several options, or make decisions that involve different domains of expertise.
The key is identifying tasks that can be meaningfully separated - each parallel sub-task should be able to operate independently and contribute a distinct piece of analysis to the final decision.
Loading

Chaining workflows might seem obvious at first, but they're actually one of the most useful patterns you'll encounter when working with Claude. This approach becomes especially valuable when you're dealing with complex tasks or long prompts that Claude struggles to handle consistently.
What is Workflow Chaining?

A chaining workflow breaks down a large, complex task into smaller, sequential subtasks. Instead of asking Claude to do everything at once, you split the work into focused steps that build on each other.

Here's a practical example: imagine you're building a social media marketing tool that creates and posts videos automatically. Rather than asking Claude to handle everything in one massive prompt, you could break it down like this:
Find related trending topics on Twitter
Select the most interesting topic (using Claude)
Research the topic (using Claude)
Write a script for a short format video (using Claude)
Use an AI avatar and text-to-speech to create a video
Post the video to social media
Why Chain Instead of One Big Prompt?

You might wonder why not just combine all the Claude tasks into a single prompt. The key benefit is focus - when you give Claude one specific task at a time, it can concentrate on doing that task well rather than juggling multiple requirements simultaneously.
The chaining approach offers several advantages:
Split large tasks into smaller, non-parallelizable subtasks
Optionally do non-LLM processing between each task
Keep Claude focused on one aspect of the overall task
The Long Prompt Problem

Here's where chaining becomes really valuable. You'll often encounter situations where you need Claude to write content with many specific constraints. Let's say you want Claude to write a technical article, and you specify that it should:
Not mention that it's written by an AI
Avoid using emojis
Skip clichéd or overly casual language
Write in a professional, technical tone

Even with all these constraints clearly stated, Claude might still produce content that violates some of your rules. You might get back an article that still uses emojis, mentions AI authorship, or sounds unprofessional.
The Chaining Solution
Instead of fighting with one massive prompt, use a two-step chaining approach:
Step 1: Send your initial prompt and accept that the first result might not be perfect. Claude will generate an article, but it might violate some of your constraints.
Step 2: Make a follow-up request that focuses specifically on fixing the issues. Provide the article Claude just wrote and give it targeted revision instructions:

Revise the article provided below. Follow these steps to rewrite the article: 1. Identify any location where the text identifies the author as an AI and remove them 2. Find and remove all emojis 3. Locate any cringey writing and replace it with text that would be written by a technical writer
This approach works because Claude can focus entirely on the revision task rather than trying to balance content creation with constraint adherence.
When to Use Chaining
Chaining workflows are particularly useful when:
You have complex tasks with multiple requirements
Claude consistently ignores some constraints in long prompts
You need to process or validate outputs between steps
You want to keep each interaction focused and manageable

While chaining might seem like extra work, it often produces better results than trying to cram everything into a single prompt. The key is recognizing when a task is complex enough to benefit from being broken down into focused, sequential steps.
Loading

Routing workflows solve a common problem in AI applications: different types of user requests need different handling approaches. Instead of using a one-size-fits-all prompt, you can categorize incoming requests and route them to specialized processing pipelines.
The Problem with Generic Prompts

Consider a social media marketing tool that generates video scripts from user topics. A user might enter "programming" or "surfing" as their topic, but these should produce very different types of content:

Programming topics call for educational content with clear explanations and definitions. Surfing topics work better with entertainment-focused scripts that emphasize excitement and visual appeal. A single generic prompt can't handle both effectively.
Setting Up Content Categories
The first step is defining the different types of content your application might need to generate. You might categorize requests into genres like:
Entertainment - High-energy, culturally relevant content with trendy language
Educational - Clear, engaging explanations with relatable examples
Comedy - Sharp, unexpected content with clever observations and timing
Personal vlog - Authentic, intimate content with conversational storytelling
Reviews - Decisive, experience-based content highlighting strengths and weaknesses
Storytelling - Immersive content using vivid details and emotional connection

Each category gets its own specialized prompt template. For example, the educational prompt might ask Claude to "develop a clear, engaging script that transforms complex information into digestible insights using relatable examples and thought-provoking questions."
How Routing Works in Practice
The routing process happens in two steps:
Categorization - Send the user's topic to Claude with a request to categorize it into one of your predefined genres
Specialized Processing - Use the category result to select the appropriate prompt template and generate content
For example, if a user enters "Python functions" as their topic, you'd first ask Claude to categorize it:
CODE:

Categorize the topic of a video into one of the listed categories: <topic>Python functions</topic> <categories> - Educational - Entertainment - Comedy - Personal vlog - Reviews - Storytelling </categories>
Claude responds with "Educational", so you then use the educational prompt template to generate the actual script content.
Routing Workflow Architecture
A routing workflow follows this pattern:
User input goes to a router component first
The router categorizes the request using an initial Claude call
Based on the category, the input gets forwarded to one specific processing pipeline
Each pipeline can have its own workflow, prompts, or tools optimized for that category
The key insight is that user input only goes to one specialized pipeline, not all of them. This allows each pipeline to be highly optimized for its specific use case.
When to Use Routing
Routing workflows work well when:
Your application handles diverse types of requests that need different approaches
You can clearly define categories that cover your use cases
The categorization step can be handled reliably by Claude
The performance benefit of specialized processing outweighs the overhead of the routing step

This pattern is especially valuable for customer service bots, content generation tools, and any application where the "right" response depends heavily on understanding the type of request being made.
Loading

Agents represent a shift from the structured workflows we've been working with. While workflows are perfect when you know the exact steps needed to complete a task, agents shine when you're not sure what those steps should be. Instead of defining a rigid sequence, you give Claude a goal and a set of tools, then let it figure out how to combine those tools to achieve the objective.

This flexibility makes agents attractive for building applications that need to handle varied, unpredictable tasks. You can create an agent once, ensure it works reasonably well, and then deploy it to solve a wide range of problems. However, this flexibility comes with trade-offs in reliability and cost that we'll explore later.
How Tools Make the Agent
The real power of agents lies in their ability to combine simple tools in unexpected ways. Consider a basic set of datetime tools:
get_current_datetime - Gets the current date and time
add_duration_to_datetime - Adds time to a given date
set_reminder - Creates a reminder for a specific time
These tools seem simple individually, but Claude can chain them together to handle surprisingly complex requests:

For "What's the time?", Claude simply calls get_current_datetime. But for "What day of the week is it in 11 days?", it chains get_current_datetime followed by add_duration_to_datetime. For setting a gym reminder next Wednesday, it might use all three tools in sequence.
Claude can even recognize when it needs more information. If you ask "When does my 90-day warranty expire?", it knows to ask when you purchased the item before calculating the expiration date.
Tools Should Be Abstract
The key insight for building effective agents is providing reasonably abstract tools rather than hyper-specialized ones. Claude Code demonstrates this principle perfectly.
Claude Code has access to generic, flexible tools like:
bash - Run any command
read - Read any file
write - Create any file
edit - Modify files
glob - Find files
grep - Search file contents

It notably doesn't have specialized tools like "refactor code" or "install dependencies." Instead, Claude figures out how to use the basic tools to accomplish these complex tasks. This abstraction allows it to handle countless programming scenarios that the developers never explicitly planned for.
Best Practice: Combinable Tools
When designing agents, provide tools that Claude can combine in creative ways. For example, a social media video agent might include:
bash - Access to FFMPEG for video processing
generate_image - Create images from prompts
text_to_speech - Convert text to audio
post_media - Upload content to social platforms

This tool set enables both simple workflows (create and post a video) and more interactive experiences where the agent might generate a sample image first, get user approval, then proceed with video creation.

The agent can adapt its approach based on user feedback and preferences, something that would be difficult to achieve with a rigid workflow. This flexibility is what makes agents powerful for building dynamic, user-responsive applications.
Loading

When building AI agents, one crucial concept often gets overlooked: environment inspection. Claude operates blindly - it needs to be able to observe and understand the results of its actions to work effectively.
Why Environment Inspection Matters

Think about how Claude works with computer use. Every time Claude performs an action like typing text or clicking a button, it immediately receives a screenshot to understand what happened. This isn't just a nice-to-have feature - it's essential.

From Claude's perspective, clicking a button could navigate to a new page, open a menu, or trigger any number of changes. Without being able to see the results, Claude has no way to understand whether its action succeeded or what the new state of the environment looks like.
Reading Before Writing

This same principle applies to file operations. Before Claude can modify any file, it needs to understand the current contents. This might seem obvious, but it's a pattern you should always follow when building agents.

In the example above, when asked to add a new route to a Python file, Claude first reads the existing code to understand the current structure. Only then can it safely make the requested changes without breaking existing functionality.
System Prompts for Environment Inspection
You can guide Claude to inspect its environment through system prompts. For complex tasks like video generation, this becomes especially important.
Consider a video creation agent that needs to:
Generate video content using tools like FFmpeg
Verify that audio dialogue is placed correctly
Check that visual elements appear as expected
You might include system prompt instructions like:
Use the bash tool to run whisper.cpp and generate caption files with timestamps to verify dialogue placement
Use FFmpeg to extract screenshots from the video at regular intervals to visually inspect the output
Compare the generated content against the original requirements
Benefits of Environment Inspection
When Claude can inspect its environment, several things improve:
Better progress tracking - Claude can gauge how close it is to completing a task
Error handling - Unexpected results can be detected and corrected
Quality assurance - Output can be verified before considering a task complete
Adaptive behavior - Claude can adjust its approach based on what it observes
Practical Implementation

When designing your own agents, always ask: "How will Claude know if this action worked?" Whether you're working with files, APIs, or user interfaces, provide tools and instructions that let Claude observe the results of its actions.
This might mean:
Reading file contents before modifications
Taking screenshots after UI interactions
Checking API responses for expected data
Validating generated content against requirements
Environment inspection transforms Claude from a blind executor of commands into an agent that can truly understand and adapt to its working environment.
Loading

When building AI-powered applications, you'll often need to choose between two different architectural approaches: workflows and agents. Each has distinct advantages and trade-offs that make them suitable for different scenarios.
What Are Workflows?

Workflows are a predefined series of calls to Claude designed to solve a known problem or set of problems. You use workflows when you can picture the flow of steps ahead of time - essentially when you know the exact sequence needed to complete a task.
Think of workflows as breaking down a big task into much smaller, more specific subtasks. Each step focuses on a single area, which allows Claude to work more precisely.
What Are Agents?

With agents, Claude gets a set of basic tools and is expected to formulate a plan to use these tools to complete a task. Unlike workflows, you don't know exactly what tasks will be provided, so the system needs to be more adaptive.
Agents can creatively figure out how to handle a wide variety of challenges by combining tools in unexpected ways.
Benefits of Workflows
Claude can focus on one subtask at a time, generally leading to higher accuracy
Far easier to evaluate and test, since you know each exact step
More predictable and reliable execution
Better suited for solving specific, well-defined problems
Benefits of Agents
Allow for more flexible user experience
Far more flexible task completion - Claude can combine tools in unexpected ways to complete a wide variety of tasks
Can handle novel situations that weren't anticipated during development
Can ask users for additional input when needed
Downsides of Workflows
Far less flexible - dedicated to solving specific types of tasks
Generally more constrained user experience - you need to know the exact inputs to the flow
Require more upfront planning and design work
Downsides of Agents
Lower successful task completion rate compared to workflows
More challenging to instrument, test, and evaluate since you often don't know what series of steps an agent will execute
Less predictable behavior
When to Use Each Approach
Your primary goal as an engineer is to solve problems reliably. Users probably don't care that you've built a fancy agent - they want a product that works consistently.

The general recommendation is to always focus on implementing workflows where possible, and only resort to agents when they are truly required. Workflows provide the reliability and predictability that most production applications need, while agents offer flexibility for scenarios where the exact requirements can't be predetermined.
Consider workflows when you have well-defined processes and agents when you need to handle unpredictable, varied user requests that require creative problem-solving.

title: Tool use with the Messages API

lines: Loading
Creating tools that Claude picks
SummaryTranscript

When Claude picks the wrong tool, look first at the tool's definition. The video follows Meridian, a fictional engineering consultancy. Meridian rewrites its tool definitions and runs the same 30 questions before and after the rewrite.
The demo in this video was recorded in September 2026. It ran on Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5). Results may differ on newer models.
Say your tool loop works, and then one of these happens:
Claude calls the wrong tool.
It makes three tool calls for one fact.
It passes 0142 where your code wants MEG-2026-0142.
Claude never receives the function that runs your tool. It sees only the definition you send and the results you return. So when Claude misuses a tool, look at the definition first.

Meridian has an internal assistant for employees' questions about projects, permits, and billing. Rewriting its tool definitions raised its score from 14 to 26 of 30 test questions, on the same model.
What Claude sees of your tool
A tool definition is a block of JSON that tells Claude a tool exists. You send it in the tools list of each request.
Here is the rewritten definition of Meridian's project tool. It has four parts.
json
CODE:

{ "name": "lookup_project_status", "description": "Returns current facts about a single Meridian …", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "project_id": { "type": "string", "description": "Full Meridian job number in the format MEG-YYYY-NNNN, e.g. MEG-2026-0142." }, "fields": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string", "enum": ["phase", "status", "lead", "hours", "deadline", "site", "client"] }, "description": "Which fields to return. Omit to return everything." } }, "required": ["project_id"] }, "input_examples": [ {"project_id": "MEG-2026-0142", "fields": ["phase", "status"]}, {"project_id": "MEG-2025-0417", "fields": ["lead", "hours"]}, {"project_id": "MEG-2024-0233"} ] }
name is what Claude calls the tool by.
description is plain text that you write and Claude reads. It's cut short here and shown in full in the next section.
input_schema lists the tool's parameters in JSON Schema, each with a name, a type, and its own description. required says which ones must be given.
input_examples is optional. It shows Claude what a good input looks like, such as a full job number. Each example must be valid against input_schema, or the API returns a 400 error.
Claude decides whether to make a tool call by reading the user's request and each tool's description.
Write a detailed description
Of the four parts, the description does the most.
Aim for at least three to four sentences, more if the tool is complex. Cover four things:
What the tool does
When to use it, and when not to
What each parameter means
What it doesn't return
Here is Meridian's full description:
text
CODE:

Returns current facts about a single Meridian project: phase, schedule status, project lead, hours budgeted and consumed, deadline, site city, and client. Use this only when the user asks about a specific project by name or job number; if only a partial number is given (e.g. 'the 0142 job'), normalize it to the full MEG-YYYY-NNNN format before calling. Pass the fields parameter to fetch just the fields the question needs instead of the whole record. This tool does not return permit or invoicing information. Use get_permit_status or get_billing_summary for those.
Meridian's description covers all four things a good description needs.

Saying when to use the tool, and when not to, helps Claude avoid calling the wrong one. Meridian's description limits the tool to questions about one project. For permits and billing, it names the tools to use.
Combine overlapping tools into one
A good description can't help much when several tools do nearly the same job.
Meridian's first set had six thin tools, each with a one-line description. Four of them returned one project fact each. Those four overlapped, so Claude had to guess which ones a question needed.

The fix is to combine the four into one tool, lookup_project_status, with a fields parameter that says which facts to return. The other two, for permits and billing, do different jobs, so they stay. Six tools become three.
Measure the change with an eval
An eval is a fixed set of test questions with known right answers, run against Claude and scored. It shows whether the new definitions are better.

Meridian's eval checks whether Claude calls the right tools. It has 30 questions an employee would ask, each labeled with the right tool calls. Meridian ran the 30 questions twice on claude-sonnet-5, once with each set of tools.
Set of toolsNumber of toolsScore
Consolidated326/30 (87%)
Fix only the part at fault
To fix one failure, find the part of the definition that's at fault, change only that part, and rerun your eval.
What Claude does wrongPart to changeWhat to do
Calls the wrong tool, or more tools than the question needsThe descriptionSay what each tool does and when to use it. Combine tools that overlap.
Passes a value of the wrong type or formatThe schema and the examplesGive the format in the parameter's own description. Add input_examples.
Troubleshooting tool use(opens in new tab) lists more symptoms and fixes.
Key takeaways
Write descriptions of at least three to four sentences, and say when not to use the tool.
Combine overlapping tools into one tool with parameters.
Measure changes with an eval.
To fix one failure, change only the part at fault.

Strict tool use: Stop rejecting your own calls
SummaryTranscript

When your backend rejects a tool call that Claude itself produced, strict tool use is the fix. The video turns it on for one tool at Meridian, a fictional engineering consultancy, and runs the same 100 requests with it off and on.
The demo in this video was recorded in September 2026. It ran on Claude Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5). Results may differ on newer models.
Claude usually follows a tool's input_schema, but nothing enforces it by default. So sometimes your backend rejects a tool call Claude made, because the call's input has one of these:
The string "2" instead of the integer 2
A missing required field
Strict tool use fixes this. One flag, strict: true, makes the input Claude writes match your schema.

At Meridian, an assistant uses the queue_stamp_request tool to queue drawing sets for a licensed engineer's stamp. Meridian's validator is the code that checks every tool call. With strict off, it rejects 79 of 100 requests. With strict on and the schema generated from the validator, it rejects none.
How strict tool use works

With strict: true, the API first compiles your JSON Schema into a grammar. A grammar is a set of rules that says which tokens may come next at each point in the input. Then, each time Claude picks the next token of the tool call, it can pick only a token that the grammar allows. This is called grammar-constrained sampling(opens in new tab).
With strict: true, only tokens your schema allows can be picked, so an integer field gets an integer.
This is Meridian's tool definition, cut down. Strict needs two of its lines, the flag and a setting the flag requires.
json
CODE:

{ "name": "queue_stamp_request", "description": "Queues a drawing set for a professional engineer's stamp.", "strict": true, "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "drawing_set_id": {"type": "string"}, "revision": {"type": "integer"} }, "required": ["drawing_set_id", "revision"], "additionalProperties": false } }
"strict": true is the flag. It sits at the top level, beside name, description, and input_schema, outside the schema.
"additionalProperties": false is the setting. It means the input can't carry a field the schema doesn't name, and strict requires it on every object.
Build the schema from your validator

Strict tool use makes the input Claude writes match your schema, so the schema must say what your validator says. When you write the schema by hand, the two drift apart. A tool call can then match the schema and still be rejected. At Meridian, a handwritten schema made the license number a plain string with no pattern. So "PE 46196" passed the schema and failed the validator, which requires PE- and five digits.
Write the rules once, in your validator, and generate the schema from it. In Python the validator is usually a Pydantic class. In TypeScript it's usually written with Zod.

Below is Meridian's Pydantic class, StampRequest, with the code that uses it, then the schema that StampRequest.model_json_schema() returns. Each # ... stands for code not shown, and the schema shows only the license number.
python
CODE:

class StampRequest(BaseModel): model_config = {"extra": "forbid"} # ... pe_license_number: str | None = Field(pattern=r"^PE-\d{5}$") # ... stamp_tool = { # ... "input_schema": StampRequest.model_json_schema(), "strict": True, } stamp_request = StampRequest.model_validate(call.input)
json
CODE:
{ "additionalProperties": false, "properties": { "pe_license_number": { "anyOf": [ {"pattern": "^PE-\\d{5}$", "type": "string"}, {"type": "null"} ], "title": "Pe License Number" } } }
"extra": "forbid" becomes "additionalProperties": false, the setting strict requires.
str | None becomes anyOf, so the license number is a string with that pattern, or null.
model_validate() checks call.input, the input Claude wrote, against the same class.
Compare the runs with strict off and on

Meridian's test sends 100 plain-language stamp requests to Claude Haiku 4.5 with the queue_stamp_request tool, and StampRequest validates every tool call. The same 100 requests run twice, first with a handwritten schema and strict off, then with the generated schema and strict on.
Replay both runs below.
Loading
The schema's pattern says what format is allowed, and strict makes Claude keep to it.

Strict controls the input's shape but can't supply a fact the request never gave. Of the 100 requests, 28 never mention a license. The generated schema allows null for the license number, and all 28 came back null.
Limits of strict tool use
Six things to know, as of November 2026:

Keep protected health information (PHI) out. Compiled schemas don't get the same PHI protections as prompts and responses, so leave PHI out of property names, enum values, const values, and pattern expressions.

Bounds aren't supported. A request whose schema uses minimum, maximum, minLength, or maxLength returns a 400 error. Check bounds in a validator function, such as Pydantic's @field_validator, and state them in the field's description.

Limits add up across tools. One request can hold at most 20 strict tools(opens in new tab). Across those tools, it can hold at most 24 optional parameters. It can also hold at most 16 parameters that use anyOf or a type array, which is what a nullable field like str | None generates.
Input can still fail to match the schema. This happens after a refusal, when a response is cut off at max_tokens, or when an enum or const string comes back in different capitalization.

Some models reject a forced tool call. Setting tool_choice to any or tool forces a tool call. That returns a 400 error on Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Mythos 5.1. On those models, leave tool_choice on auto, its default.
Programmatic tool calling can't use strict tools. In programmatic tool calling, Claude writes code that calls your tools. Lesson 8 covers it.
Key takeaways
strict: true makes tool input match your schema, except after a refusal or a cut-off response, or when an enum or const string changes case.
Generate the schema from your validator, such as a Pydantic class.
Keep bounds out of the schema, and count tools, optional parameters, and nullable parameters across the whole request.

Parallel tool calling: Cut the latency
SummaryTranscript

Claude can ask for several tools in one response, and your code can run them together. The video checks a job site for Meridian, a fictional engineering consultancy. One tool call at a time takes 19.9 seconds, while parallel tool calls take 10.8.
The demo in this video was recorded in September 2026. It ran on Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5). Results may differ on newer models.
Running tool calls one at a time makes your user wait for each one in turn.

When the tools that Claude wants don't depend on each other, it can ask for them all in one response. Claude does this by default, so your loop has to handle every tool call and send a result back for each one.
Three tool calls in one response
Parallel tool use means one response holds several tool_use blocks.

Meridian has a Python script that checks whether a job site is ready for fieldwork. The site check needs three lookups that don't depend on each other: the project's status, the weather at the site, and the state of the permit.
Here is Claude's response to Meridian's site check, with one tool_use block for each tool it wants.
json
CODE:

{ "role": "assistant", "stop_reason": "tool_use", "content": [ {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "get_project_status", "input": {"job_number": "MEG-2026-0142"}}, {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_02", "name": "get_site_weather", "input": {"site": "Riverside"}}, {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_03", "name": "get_permit_state", "input": {"permit_id": "P-88213"}} ] }
The response's stop_reason is tool_use, and each tool call has its own id.
Run every tool call

A loop written for one tool call reads only the first tool_use block. It sends back one result, two tool calls never get theirs, and the API rejects the request. So collect every tool_use block in the response.
python
CODE:
calls = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
Next, run those tool calls at the same time. Each lookup spends most of its time waiting on another system. Give each one its own thread, and the three waits overlap instead of adding up.
python
CODE:
with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool: results = list(pool.map(run_tool, calls))
run_tool runs one tool call and returns its result, and the next two sections build it.

Running tool calls at the same time is usually safe when they only read data and don't depend on each other, like Meridian's lookups. When tools change data, or must go in a set order, it might be better to run them one after another.
Send every result back in one message
Once the three tool calls have run, Claude is waiting for their results. Each result goes back in a tool_result block, and its tool_use_id holds the id of the tool call it answers.
python
CODE:
result = {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id}
Every tool_use block gets one tool_result, and they all go in the next user message.
python
CODE:
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content}) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
One user message with all three results keeps Claude calling tools in parallel.
If your loop sends each result in its own message instead, the conversation reads as if Claude had asked for one tool at a time. That is a common reason Claude makes fewer parallel tool calls.
Return an error result for a bad tool call
Running three tool calls at once means one can fail while the other two succeed. If your code raises an exception and nothing catches it, your loop stops, and the two good results are lost with it.
So send the failure back as a result. It's an ordinary tool_result with the error message as its content, plus is_error: true. The message should say what went wrong and what Claude should try next.
python
CODE:
try: result["content"] = HANDLERS[call.name](**call.input) except Exception as exc: result["content"] = f"{call.name} failed: {exc}" result["is_error"] = True
HANDLERS is a dict from tool names to the Python functions that do each tool's work. Each function returns a string, because a tool_result's content is a string or a list of content blocks.
Put the loop together
The snippets above fit into Meridian's loop below. The script has already set up client, tools, prompt, and HANDLERS.
Loading
Key takeaways
Run every tool call in a response, and run them at the same time when they don't depend on each other.
Send back one tool_result for each tool call, and put them all in one user message.
Don't send each result in its own message, because that reduces parallel tool use.
Send a failure back as a result with is_error: true, so one bad tool call doesn't stop the loop.

Streaming tool calls: No more frozen spinners
SummaryTranscript

A streamed tool call arrives with the tool's name first and its input in pieces, so the screen can say what is happening. The video shows two versions of the screen at Meridian, a fictional engineering consultancy, side by side. One has no streaming and the other has streaming. The demo is simulated and runs at one-third speed.
This video was recorded in September 2026, and its code uses Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5). Your results may differ on newer models.
Say your user watches a spinner for eight seconds. That happens because your tool loop sends each request, waits, and gets back a finished response.

In that time Claude picks a tool and writes its input, your code runs the tool, and Claude writes the answer. Your code sees each response only once it is finished, so your UI has nothing to show while Claude writes.

Meridian has this problem today. Its support agent is written in Python and answers employees' questions about projects. When an employee asks "What's the status of the pump station job?" the screen says "thinking..." until the answer comes.

Streaming changes what that employee sees. With streaming, your code gets the response piece by piece, before it is finished. So Meridian's screen can say "Looking up project..." as soon as Claude picks the tool.
What a streamed tool call looks like

Where your tool loop sends its request, replace client.messages.create(...) with client.messages.stream(...)(opens in new tab). The response then arrives as a series of server-sent events(opens in new tab), small JSON messages that each have a type.

A response is made of content blocks, or blocks for short, with one block for each stretch of Claude's text and one for each tool call. A tool call's block has the type tool_use. Current models can also add thinking blocks, which this lesson's code ignores.

Picture a friend reading you a phone number over the phone. First they tell you whose number it is: "Here's the plumber's number." Then they read it out a few digits at a time, stopping wherever they like. Finally they say "That's it."
A tool call's block arrives the way the phone number did. One event opens it, one or more events fill it, and one event closes it. Here are the events of Meridian's tool call.
text
CODE:

{"type": "content_block_start", "index": 0, "content_block": {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "lookup_project_status", "input": {}}} {"type": "content_block_delta", "index": 0, "delta": {"type": "input_json_delta", "partial_json": "{\"project_"}} {"type": "content_block_delta", "index": 0, "delta": {"type": "input_json_delta", "partial_json": "id\": \"MEG-2"}} {"type": "content_block_delta", "index": 0, "delta": {"type": "input_json_delta", "partial_json": "026-0142\"}"}} {"type": "content_block_stop", "index": 0}
Show the chosen tool as soon as its block opens
The tool's name is in content_block_start, the block's first event. When that event arrives, your code can update the status line, the one line of text your UI shows while your user waits.
Meridian keeps a small dict, STATUS, that maps each tool's name to words for the user, so lookup_project_status becomes "Looking up project..." on the screen.
Put the streaming request together
When the stream ends, call stream.get_final_message() to get the finished response, the same kind of object that client.messages.create(...) returns. So the rest of your tool loop stays as it was.
Here is Meridian's streaming request. on_status is a function you write that shows a string as the status line.
Loading
Key takeaways
A streamed tool call arrives with the tool's name first, then its input in pieces.
As soon as content_block_start arrives, show the chosen tool in words your user understands.
stream.get_final_message() returns the finished response, so the rest of your tool loop doesn't change.

Code execution: Claude runs the code it writes
SummaryTranscript
Code execution lets Claude write Python, run it on Anthropic's side, and answer from what it prints.
The demo in this video was recorded in September 2026. It ran on Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5). Results may differ on newer models.
Some questions need math across many files. That's a job for code.

Take Meridian, a fictional engineering consultancy. It has 12 CSV files, one for each pump station, and each file holds a year of flow readings. It wants to know whether any station ever went over its design capacity, and if so, when.
Code execution is how Claude does that job. Claude gets a container where it can run the Python it writes and answer from what the code prints.
Add the tool to your request
Code execution is a server tool, a tool that runs on Anthropic's infrastructure. You write no handler for it, and your code sends back no tool_result.

Adding code execution takes one entry in your tools list. The date at the end of the entry's type is the tool's version, and Meridian uses code_execution_20260120. The current versions are listed in the Tool reference(opens in new tab), so copy the type value from there.
Meridian keeps the list in a constant named TOOLS, and its request passes it as tools=TOOLS:
python
CODE:
TOOLS = [{"type": "code_execution_20260120", "name": "code_execution"}]

As of October 2026, code execution(opens in new tab) runs on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, the Claude models on Google Cloud that Anthropic manages, and Microsoft Foundry deployments hosted on Anthropic.
Put your files in the container
Claude's code runs in a container on Anthropic's side. Your files are still on your machine, so the container doesn't have them yet. Meridian's program gets them into the container in two steps:
Upload each file with the Files API(opens in new tab), which gives you back a file ID.
Put that file ID in your message, in a container_upload block.
Meridian's program adds one container_upload block for each file, in the same message as its question. The files are then loaded onto the container, where Claude's code can open them.
Read Claude's answer
Your code sends one request and usually gets back the finished answer.
The API can pause a long-running turn and return a stop_reason of pause_turn. When it does, send the response's content back as an assistant message, with the same tools, and Claude continues.
Claude's answer for Meridian is that Station 7 went over its design capacity of 600 L/s twice, in April and May 2025. In the response, the answer comes after the commands Claude ran.
Put the program together

Meridian's program below adds the tool, puts the files in the container, and reads the answer. In the program, paths holds the 12 CSV files as pathlib.Path objects, and QUESTION holds Meridian's question.

Key takeaways
Code execution is a server tool. You add one entry to tools, and Claude's code runs in a container on Anthropic's side.
You upload each file with the Files API, then put its file ID in a container_upload block.

Web search: Answers from the sites you trust
SummaryTranscript

The web search tool lets Claude search the web while it works on your request. Dynamic filtering keeps only the relevant parts of the search results, so you use fewer tokens on search-heavy requests. Meridian, a fictional engineering consultancy, cites engineering standards in its proposals.
The demo in this video was recorded in September 2026. It ran on Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5). Results may differ on newer models.

Claude answers from what it learned in training, so it doesn't know about anything newer than that, or anything that was never in it. When a question needs those facts, someone has to look them up, and that legwork falls to you.
With the web search tool, Claude does that legwork itself, searching the web while it works on your request and answering from what it finds.

One of Meridian's proposals cites four Canadian engineering standards by clause, and Meridian carries professional liability if any reference is wrong. So before the proposal goes out, Meridian wants each reference checked against official sources.
Add the tool to your request
Web search is a server tool. It runs on Anthropic's infrastructure, so you don't write a handler for it or send back a tool_result.

Adding it takes one entry in your tools list. The entry's type picks the version of the tool, and Meridian sets it to web_search_20260209. Its name is always web_search. The tool reference(opens in new tab) lists the current versions, so copy the type value from there.

On Claude 4.6 and later models, web_search_20260209 and later versions use dynamic filtering by default. Claude runs code that filters the search results, so only relevant content reaches the context window.
Claude usually does all its searching during one request. Your code sends that request and gets back the finished answer.
The API can pause a long-running turn and return a stop_reason of pause_turn. When it does, send the response's content back as an assistant message, with the same tools, and Claude continues.
Each search is billed(opens in new tab) on top of what you pay for tokens. Not every cloud platform offers web search(opens in new tab).
Name the sites Claude may use

So far, nothing in the request limits which sites Claude can search, and that's a problem for Meridian. The open web is full of forum posts and reseller sites, but Meridian can stand behind only official sources.

So you tell the search where it may look. allowed_domains is another field in the tool's entry, and it limits search results to the sites you name. Meridian names four sites. Two belong to the bodies that publish these standards and certify to them, csagroup.org and cwbgroup.org. Two belong to governments, ontario.ca and canada.ca.
allowed_domains takes a list. Write each item as a bare domain with no https://, and its subdomains are included.
Read the answer and its sources
Claude's answer can arrive in several text blocks, with the searches in between. So join every text block to get the whole answer.
Each search also adds a web_search_tool_result block to the response. It holds the list of results the search returned, and each result has a title and a url.
Of Meridian's four references, Claude found that two check out, a third checks out except for its subclause number, and the fourth is wrong.
Put the program together
Meridian's program puts these steps together. In the program, excerpt holds the passage from the proposal, and QUESTION holds Meridian's question.
Loading
Key takeaways
Web search is a server tool, so you add one entry to tools and don't write a handler. Claude usually does all its searching during one request.
allowed_domains limits search results to the sites you name.
On Claude 4.6 and later models, dynamic filtering is on by default in web_search_20260209 and later versions, so only relevant content reaches the context window.
Most companies have at least one app with no API at all. The tools from the earlier lessons can't reach it, because there's nothing for them to call.

Meridian, a fictional engineering consultancy, has one of these apps. It's an old drawing manager called PlotDesk, also fictional. Every Friday, one person spends the day clicking through the same screens to export PDF plot sets. PlotDesk has no API and no command line. It has only windows and buttons.
Computer use lets Claude operate PlotDesk through those windows and buttons, just as a person would, by looking at screenshots and deciding what to click and which text to type.
Meridian wants Claude to export today's PDF plot set for project MEG-2026-0142.
See who carries out each action

Through the API, Claude never connects to the desktop. All Claude produces is a response with tool calls in it. Your program is the Python program that calls the Messages API. It carries out each action on the desktop and sends back the result.

Here's the loop. Claude asks for a screenshot. Your program takes one and sends it back as an image. Claude looks at it and sends the next action, such as a click at given coordinates or some text to type. Your program carries out the action, and the loop repeats until the task is done. It's the tool loop you already have, except that some of the results are screenshots.
Meridian's whole export took seven actions.
Claude's actionWhat happened
screenshotClaude finds the PlotDesk window
left_clickOn the Project number field
typeMEG-2026-0142
left_clickOn Open
screenshotPlotDesk shows the project: Pump Station Replacement, 22 sheets
left_clickOn Export PDF
screenshotThe status bar reads "Exported MEG-2026-0142_plots.pdf"
Run the desktop in a dedicated container

Claude acts on whatever is on the screen. Text in a web page or an image can override your instructions or lead Claude into mistakes. To limit how much harm one wrong action can do, give the desktop a dedicated container or virtual machine that holds only what the task needs. Set it up this way:
Each session gets a dedicated container.
The container holds no credentials and no directories mounted from the host.
The container can reach only the network hosts the task uses.
Your program and your API key stay outside the container.
Write the actions, and let the SDK run the loop

The Python and TypeScript SDKs have a class called the computer toolset. You subclass it and write one method for each action the task needs. The class builds the toolset's tools entry for you and is in beta. In Python, it needs version 1.12.0 or later of the SDK.
Meridian implements three of the toolset's actions: screenshot, left_click, and type. Any action you don't implement is sent to the API as disabled.

Each method is one line that hands the work to backend. That's your own wrapper around whatever controls the desktop, such as a VNC client or xdotool. This minimal VNC example in Python and TypeScript(opens in new tab) is a good place to start, but it isn't meant for production.
Pass an instance of your class in tools, along with the prompt. Tool Runner, an SDK helper, runs the loop for you until Claude replies without a tool call.

As of November 2026, this toolset(opens in new tab) is available on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry. The models that support it vary by platform. Meridian's program below calls the Claude API, so on another platform, use that platform's SDK client and model ID. Some older models, such as Claude Opus 4.7, have only the earlier beta tool versions. Those take a different tools entry and a beta header, a request header that turns on a beta feature.
Have a person approve clicks and typing

When you create the instance, pass a function called confirm. The SDK calls it before every action. If it returns True, the action runs. Anything else refuses the action, and Claude is told that a person turned it down.

confirm sees the action and its input, but not the screen. A person watching the desktop can see what sits at the point Claude wants to click. So Meridian approves screenshots automatically and sends every click and every type action to its operator, the person watching the desktop.

Here's Meridian's program. Three names in it come from Meridian's own code, not the SDK: backend, ask_operator, and TASK. ask_operator shows the operator the action and returns their answer, and TASK holds the prompt.
Loading
Decide when computer use fits

Every screenshot stays in the conversation, so each step costs more than the one before. So when the software has an MCP server (a service that offers its functions to Claude as tools), an API, or a command line, use that instead. Computer use is for software that has none of these, like PlotDesk.
If the task stays inside web pages, the browser use tool(opens in new tab) is the closer fit. It reads and acts on the page itself and needs no full desktop.
Key takeaways
Claude asks for actions, and your program carries them out.
The desktop runs in a dedicated container for each session.
You implement only the actions the task needs.
Meridian's confirm function sends every click and every type action to a person to approve.
Use a direct interface when one exists, and computer use when none does.

Cut the cost of tool-heavy workflows
SummaryTranscript
An agent that uses tools sends everything again on every request. Programmatic tool calling and prompt caching each cut a different part of its cost.
The demo in this video was recorded in September 2026. It ran on Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5). Results may differ on newer models.

An agent that uses tools sends everything again on every request, so its cost grows with each tool call. Each request carries the tool definitions, the system prompt, the question, and every tool result so far. Those are its input tokens, and each one is billed.
Programmatic tool calling and prompt caching both cut that cost.

Meridian is a fictional engineering consultancy with 40 engineers. Its agent got one question: Which engineers were under 70% utilization in June 2026? The agent had two tools. list_employees returns the roster, and get_employee_hours returns one engineer's timesheet.
Answering that question took the agent 42 requests and 1,124,799 input tokens. The whole run cost $2.29 in tokens.
Measure the input tokens in each request
Print usage.input_tokens each time a response comes back, because those counts show you where the cost is.
python
CODE:
resp = client.messages.create(...) print(resp.usage.input_tokens, "input tokens")
Meridian's agent runs a classic loop, where each response asks for one tool call. Here are two of its counts.
RequestWhat it carriesInput tokens
Request 1Tool definitions, system prompt, and question606
Request 37The same, plus 36 earlier tool results47,905
Request 1 carries only what every request sends. Later requests add tool calls and their results. Compare the two counts to see which part grew.
Keep tool results out of what Claude reads

With programmatic tool calling(opens in new tab), Claude writes a script that calls your tools, and the code execution tool runs it in a container. Only what the script prints reaches Claude. Meridian's 40 timesheets stay with the script, and Claude gets its short printout.

Check your tools and your model first. As of October 2026, programmatic tool calling doesn't support tools marked strict: true(opens in new tab). It also doesn't support disable_parallel_tool_use, the tool_choice setting that limits Claude to one tool call in each response. tool_choice can't force Claude to call a tool from the script.
Claude Haiku 4.5 doesn't support the feature. The feature runs on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, and Microsoft Foundry deployments hosted on Anthropic.
Turning on programmatic tool calling takes four changes.
Add the code execution tool to your tools list.
Mark the tools the script may call. Give each one an allowed_callers field that names the code execution tool at version code_execution_20260120 or later(opens in new tab).
Send the container's ID back. Read it from each response that stops for a tool call, and send it with the request that returns your tool results.
Describe each tool's result. Say in the description what shape it takes, because the script has to parse it. Here's Meridian's description for get_employee_hours.
Returns one engineer's hours for the month as JSON: {"name": str, "billable_hours": float, "utilization": float 0-1}
Here's Meridian's loop after these changes.
python
CODE:

CODE_EXECUTION = "code_execution_20260120" TOOLS = [ {"type": CODE_EXECUTION, "name": "code_execution"}, {**LIST_EMPLOYEES, "allowed_callers": [CODE_EXECUTION]}, {**GET_EMPLOYEE_HOURS, "allowed_callers": [CODE_EXECUTION]}, ] messages = [{"role": "user", "content": QUESTION}] container = None while True: resp = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=4096, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages, container=container, ) print(resp.usage.input_tokens, "input tokens") if resp.stop_reason not in ("tool_use", "pause_turn"): break container = resp.container.id messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content}) if resp.stop_reason == "tool_use": messages.append({"role": "user", "content": run_tools(resp)}) print("".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text"))
LIST_EMPLOYEES and GET_EMPLOYEE_HOURS are Meridian's tool definitions.
Your own run_tools runs each tool call and returns the results.
On pause_turn, the loop sends the response back and continues.

When the script calls a tool, the response's stop_reason is "tool_use". Your code runs the tool, and the result goes to the script, not to Claude. The script can run tools in parallel, so one response can hold more than one tool call.
Here's the same question answered both ways.
RunRequestsTool callsInput tokensToken cost
Programmatic tool calling34128,486$0.0667
Both runs used the same question, the same tools, and claude-sonnet-5. Costs use prices as of September 2026(opens in new tab), and code execution time is billed separately from tokens.
Programmatic tool calling fits lookups that don't depend on each other. It helps little when Claude has to reason over each result before it makes the next tool call.
Cache tool definitions that repeat
With prompt caching, the API stores the prefix of your request, the part up to a cache point you mark. Reading that prefix again costs far less.
A second Meridian agent has 14 tools, and their definitions come to 3,305 tokens that every request sends again.
Mark the cache point by putting cache_control on the last tool, and the whole list is cached. That takes one line:
python
CODE:
TOOLS[-1]["cache_control"] = {"type": "ephemeral"}
On Claude Sonnet 5, reading the prefix costs a tenth of the normal input price(opens in new tab). Writing it costs 1.25 times the normal input price.

The cached prefix lasts five minutes by default, and each use renews it. For requests further apart, add "ttl": "1h" to cache_control to keep it for an hour. Writing a one-hour cache costs twice the normal input price(opens in new tab).
Meridian ran the same eight questions with the cache and without it. Its total input cost fell from $0.0554 to $0.0154.
With automatic caching(opens in new tab), you put one cache_control field at the top level of the request, and the API places the cache point for you.
Watch for three things once caching is on:
Change any tool definition and you lose the whole cache.
On Sonnet 5, a cached prefix has to be at least 1,024 tokens. When it's shorter, nothing is cached and no error says so.
With caching on, input_tokens leaves out the cached prefix, so a request's true total is input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens added together.
Combine the features where they fit
Add them in this order.
Start with caching. It takes one line.
Test programmatic tool calling. Run some of your usual traffic with and without allowed_callers, then compare each run's billed input tokens.
For each of the two Meridian requests below, find the part that holds most of the input tokens, then pick the feature that cuts it.
Loading
Key takeaways
Every request sends everything again, so you pay for old tool results over and over.
Print usage.input_tokens each time a response comes back, so you know which part of the request costs the most.
Start with caching. Add cache_control to the last tool in your list.
When your tool calls don't depend on each other, set up programmatic tool calling with the code execution tool and allowed_callers. Send the container's ID with every later request.

What you can do now
Get tool calls right. Describe when to call each tool and when not to, test with an eval, and turn on strict tool use.
Shorten the wait and show what's happening. Run independent tool calls in parallel, and stream so users see which tool Claude chose while they wait.
Use the tools Anthropic provides. Add code execution and web search, which run on Anthropic's side, and keep computer use for software with no other way in.
Spend less. Measure the input tokens in each request, cache your tool definitions, and use programmatic tool calling.

Claude is more than a chatbot—it's an AI assistant designed to be your thinking partner. In this lesson you'll learn what makes Claude different from other AI tools and see how it can help with a wide variety of work tasks.
Key takeaways

Claude is an AI assistant for life and work: At a high level, Claude is guided by principles that help it avoid toxic or discriminatory outputs, avoid helping humans engage in illegal or unethical activities, and broadly behave as a safe and beneficial AI system. This approach, called Constitutional AI, means Claude is trained to align with human values and operate transparently.

Claude is more than a chatbot: Claude is capable of a wide variety of conversational and text processing tasks while maintaining a high degree of reliability and predictability, including summarization, search, creative and collaborative writing, Q&A, coding, and more. Think of Claude as a thinking partner who can help you tackle complex problems, and work through challenging situations, not just answer simple questions.

Claude is designed to be steerable and collaborative: Claude can take direction on personality, tone, and behavior, and customers report that Claude is much less likely to produce harmful outputs, easier to converse with, and more steerable—so you can get your desired output with less effort.

You can access Claude wherever you work: Claude apps are available to all plan types: Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise. Your conversations, projects, memory, and preferences sync across all devices when you're signed in. Whether you're at your desk or on the go, Claude is available through web, desktop, and mobile apps.

Claude can help with a wide range of tasks that go far beyond simple question-and-answer interactions to assistant-like partnership that can both automate and augment your work.

Getting started with Claude.ai

Imagine this: you're looking at a blank page, wrestling with a big, complex project, and not sure where to start. What if you had a partner who could help you break it down? Claude is a powerful, intelligent collaborator that amplifies your capabilities across all of your work. Claude brings AI intelligence, but you bring the context and expertise that makes the work meaningful.

Let's explore chatting with Claude, beginning with the sidebar. Here you will encounter icons for creating new chats and jumping back into old ones. There are options for projects where you can organize your conversations with persistent context and custom instructions, and then artifacts which allow you to turn ideas into shareable apps, tools, or content. No matter what you hope to accomplish, Claude offers support to achieve your goals.

All interactions with Claude begin with a prompt, and these prompts, combined with other context, impact its response. The best approach when speaking to Claude is like you would a coworker: naturally, concisely, and conversational. But you may ask, what is a good prompt?

Before your next conversation with Claude, consider a few things. One, setting the stage. What is your role and what are your objectives? Is there context about your work that Claude should know about? Two, defining the task. What action do you want Claude to take? Do you want Claude to write, analyze, build, etc.? Three, specifying rules. Is there a style or tone you want Claude to use? Are there examples that you can attach to show Claude?

Let's review this prompt below. First, we're setting the stage by telling Claude this is for an investor pitch deck for a new indie streaming app. That's the context and the objective. Then, we define the task clearly by providing relevant details. Finally, we specify the rules by using current web research with citations, structuring it as a professional report, which tells Claude exactly what style and format we need. Perfect.

With your basic prompt in place, now comes the real power move: adding your specific context to make Claude's response truly tailored to your needs. When you upload relevant documents or background information into a specific chat, Claude considers that context in its response, whether that's company documents, project files, or background research. Think of it as a shortcut so that Claude can understand what your needs are. Claude can intake and output many file types such as PDF, CSV, docs, and more.

In the search and tools menu, you can level up your experience yet again by giving Claude access to more tools, to pull in more context, and it will pull in these tools as needed while solving your request. You might toggle on options like web search to let Claude research current market data, or use connected data sources to pull from Google Drive, allowing access to real-time information. Claude will choose the right approach.

While those options directly impact the information Claude has access to, there are a few more ways to customize how Claude responds. You could choose the best Claude model for your task. To use the model selector, start chatting with Claude or open an existing chat. The selected model will appear under your text input. To change it, click on the model name and choose which model of Claude you'd like to chat with instead. Changing the model will result in a new chat.

Claude currently supports numerous models with distinct capabilities intended to meet specific user's needs. Use the Claude Opus model for your most complex tasks. It's the largest scale model with hybrid reasoning capabilities, for example, running a multi-step financial analysis. Claude Sonnet is the best choice for everyday users and is our recommended default model. It balances sophisticated capabilities with cost effectiveness. Think of it like choosing the right tool for the job. You can always switch models based on what you're trying to accomplish.

Extended thinking mode is particularly valuable for complex thinking and analysis, though it increases latency and may not be necessary for simple questions and everyday conversations. To get the fastest output for more straightforward tasks, you can start with Sonnet models and leave thinking mode off. If you need more support, you can change the model or turn on thinking mode.

Claude Sonnet enables Claude to conduct systematic multi-angle investigations by automatically breaking down complex questions and exploring hundreds of sources to deliver comprehensive, cited reports in five to 45 minutes. Claude does the research for you while you focus on other high-value work.

Now just wait as Claude delivers to you a well-crafted response that effectively accomplishes your task. But the real power of Claude comes with continued and frequent communication, not just one-off prompts. The more you interact with Claude, the better it becomes at understanding your communication style and preferences for future conversations.

Working with Claude, you have a great partner and a powerful intelligent collaborator that amplifies your capabilities across everything you work on. Claude brings AI intelligence to your work. You bring the context and expertise that makes the work meaningful.

Writing effective prompts
All interactions with Claude begin with a prompt, and these prompts, combined with other context, impact Claude's response. Write your prompt as if you were talking to a coworker.
But you may ask, what is a good prompt? Before your next conversation with Claude, consider a few things:
Setting the stage: What is your role and what are your objectives? Is there context about your work that Claude should know about?
Defining the task: What action do you want Claude to take? Do you want Claude to write, analyze, build, or something else?
Specifying rules: What's the style or tone you want Claude to use? Are there examples that you can attach to show Claude what you're looking for?
Putting it together
Here's an example prompt that uses all three elements:

I'm the marketing lead at an indie streaming startup, and we're preparing an investor pitch deck for Series A investors. Can you research the current state of the independent film streaming market and identify key trends, competitor positioning, and growth opportunities? Use current web research with citations and structure it as a professional report of up to 5 pages, with an executive summary, market analysis, competitive landscape, and growth opportunities.
In this prompt:
Prompt
Setting the stage. We tell Claude this is for an investor pitch deck for an indie streaming startup. That's the context and objective.
Prompt
Defining the task. We provide the specific action (research the market) with relevant details (trends, competitors, opportunities).
Prompt
Specifying rules. We ask for current web research with citations, structured as a professional report—telling Claude exactly what style and format we need.

Want to go deeper? This prompt framework is adapted from the 4D Framework for AI Fluency, developed through research collaboration between Professor Rick Dakan (Ringling College of Art and Design) and Professor Joseph Feller (University College Cork). The framework identifies four core competencies—Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence—that enable effective collaboration with AI.
